title: Security Misconfiguration
subtitle: Default credentials, exposed debug endpoints, verbose error messages, and production hardening checklist

content.code:
DEFAULT CREDENTIALS:
  Database installed with root/admin + no password (MySQL, MongoDB, Redis)
  Admin panels with admin/admin or admin/password (Jenkins, Grafana, phpMyAdmin)
  Cloud services with default IAM policies (wide-open S3 buckets)
  Fix: change all defaults before connecting to any network

EXPOSED DEBUG ENDPOINTS:
  /debug, /status, /metrics — internal endpoints publicly accessible
  Spring Boot Actuator /actuator/env exposing environment variables
  Rails /rails/info/properties in production
  GraphQL introspection enabled in production (reveals full schema)
  Fix: disable in production, restrict to internal network / VPN IP ranges

VERBOSE ERROR MESSAGES:
  Stack traces with file paths, library versions, internal IPs in production
  SQL errors exposing table/column names: 'column password_hash does not exist'
  Fix: catch all errors, log internally, return generic messages to clients

DIRECTORY LISTING:
  Web server configured to show file lists for directories without index.html
  Exposes source files, config files, uploaded documents
  Fix: disable in nginx (autoindex off;) and Apache (Options -Indexes)

UNNECESSARY OPEN PORTS:
  Database port 5432 (PostgreSQL) exposed to public internet
  Redis port 6379 open — Redis has no auth by default
  Fix: firewall rules to allow database access only from app servers
  Cloud: security groups should only allow necessary traffic

questions.question: Your production API returns this error: 'PG::UndefinedColumn: ERROR: column users.password_hash does not exist'. What security issues does this expose?
options: None — it's just a database error, not a security issue
It reveals that you use PostgreSQL (PG::), the table name (users), a column name (password_hash), and that the app has a bug an attacker can probe — all useful reconnaissance information
It only reveals that there's a bug, which is public knowledge once the error is visible
It exposes the password hash of a user
questions.explanation: This error message is free reconnaissance. It tells an attacker: (1) you're using PostgreSQL (PG:: prefix — they know which SQL injection syntax to use); (2) there's a table called 'users'; (3) there's (or was) a column called 'password_hash' — they now know how your auth schema is structured; (4) there's a bug they can potentially probe further. In production, this should be caught and logged internally, while the client receives only 'Something went wrong'. The detailed error goes to your logging service (Pino/Sentry), not the HTTP response. Remove X-Powered-By header for the same reason — don't give attackers a free fingerprint.

faq.q: How do I make sure debug configuration is never accidentally deployed to production?
faq.a: Gate all debug behavior on NODE_ENV checks, and enforce that NODE_ENV=production in your deployment environment via your hosting platform's environment variable config (Railway, Render, Vercel, etc.). Never hardcode NODE_ENV in your committed code — set it in the deployment environment. For extra safety, use a separate startup script for production that validates required env vars and fails fast if debug flags are set. Many teams also run configuration audits as part of their CI pipeline.

examples: In 2017, a misconfigured Amazon S3 bucket belonging to a defense contractor exposed 1.8 billion scraped social media posts and 400GB of sensitive data. The bucket was set to public-read. AWS has since added 'Block Public Access' features and alerts for public buckets, but misconfigured cloud storage remains one of the most common causes of data breaches

The 2020 SolarWinds supply chain attack involved attackers who had persistent access exploiting a misconfigured build system. Attackers had been present for months before detection. One contributing factor: insufficient internal network segmentation and overly permissive internal access controls meant that once inside, they could move freely. Defense-in-depth (principle of least privilege, network segmentation) limits blast radius when prevention fails
